1598665511973306368 [2022-12-02] @forthrighter 💜 4
there's a cognitive attack I've heard of called "smuggled assumption" where someone throws 20 statements up against the wall and such an array of different ideas to deal with that people miss & subsequently swallow an unstated assumption https://t.co/UaDhW4vb62
  [Quoting Tweet 1598555216093118464 (missing)]
↓
1598665893252317184 [2022-12-02] @forthrighter 💜 1
example nonsense:

NASA is lying to us, world is flat
...but even if it isn't, still gov't is hiding data
...which X politician supported
(etc etc etc)

doesn't matter if you believe any of that, smuggled assumption is "institutions aren't trustworthy"
↓
1598666216905785345 [2022-12-02] @forthrighter 💜 1
smuggled assumptions work on the bullshit asymmetry principle (BSAP). The more arguments, the less likely you will ever be to actually slow down and actually disentangle wtf is going on (and hence you are less likely to discover the smuggled assumption) https://t.co/fDXapNykAF
  [Quoting @forthrighter: @Morphenius what's different about the meme world? Chiefly that it's so high speed & high volume, it actively makes the classic defense even less feasible than it already was, because of the bullshit asymmetry principle https://t.co/9ivG3i3tyB]
↓
1598666388167692290 [2022-12-02] @forthrighter 
it's also possible to make lots of errors very quickly, in a small compact form.  Here's a tiny sentence with a bunch of errors/smuggled assumptions (this example more funny than sinister)

https://t.co/No3XXIe08p
  [Quoting @forthrighter: I have been weirdly fascinated for years with one small Beastie Boys lyric  "dropping science like Galileo dropped the orange "  because of what it implies about rhetoric and art🧵 https://t.co/8wk5q3cTsQ]
↓
1598666713569980416 [2022-12-02] @forthrighter  [(SEED) type=semantic_search]
defense against this particular dark art is really tough.  Leading defense is to categorically discount everything speaker is saying without consideration; for practical time reasons, you can understand why that's the go-to.

https://t.co/8L82YNxUpj

rating.reasoning_summary: This strand centers on the boundary object of 'epistemic self-defense'—specifically, the practice of refusing persuasion attempts rather than engaging with them dialectically. Beginning with scattered observations about belief-cosplay (2020) and frame control (2022-2023), it crystallizes around eigenrobot's viral 'that's crazy bro' tweet (Dec 2023), which becomes a memetic artifact for rejecting persuasion without justification. The discourse is primarily constructive rather than dialectical: participants build on each other's insights about permission structures for belief-updating, local optima in worldviews, and the asymmetry between persuasion and truth. The strand shows medium evolution (from abstract observations to tactical heuristics) but lacks real-world execution or institutional artifacts.

title: “That’s crazy bro” as a mental firewall
summary:
The most quotable takeaway was @eigenrobot’s: the best defense against persuasion “dark arts” is to notice someone is trying to move you and just refuse—no debate, no justification. His viral Dec 31 tweet turns “that’s crazy bro” into a memetic get-out-of-argument-free card, with a perfect reaction-image of a guy casually stonewalling an interviewer (“this guy gets it”). The core claim isn’t “never update,” it’s “stop granting strangers admin access to your belief-evaluator by default.”

The arc starts as scattered epistemic-defense vibes: @nosilverv frames “unintentional gaslighting” as people lacking “root access” to their own beliefs (2020), @GeniesLoki adds “people cosplay beliefs,” and @forthrighter describes “smuggled assumptions” + bullshit asymmetry: too many claims at once forces you to swallow an unstated premise, so the practical defense becomes “categorically discount everything.” In early 2023, eigenrobot sharpens it into a tactic: arguing with absurd claims is a failure mode; refuse to take them seriously, maybe even point out the speaker doesn’t believe it either—“this will make them mad” / “that’s fine.” @mykola escalates the vibe into an almost-combative warning: people who insist “don’t fight back, just persuade them” are “trying to get you killed,” i.e., moralizing you into unilateral vulnerability.

The peak is the Dec 2023 explosion where eigenrobot justifies the refusal philosophically: “most novel ideas are harmful,” you’re near a “local optimum,” and letting people argue at you is like giving them “rwx permissions” to your mind—there are “human and inhuman actors” treating you as a resource, and even your trusted people can be “psyoped.” @vividvoid wraps it into a status ladder (“Bespoke: recognizing the pattern and refraining from participation”), while @Malcolm_Ocean offers the more socially-polite cousin move: “that may be so, but I don’t care” (accepting someone’s claim without letting it steer you). After the meme, the thread kind of diffuses into applications and mild pushback: @georgejrjrjr suggests “shit testing” frame-controllers by reflecting understanding before rejecting them; later, @rikardhjort ports it to politics as “incredulity” (“oh wow huh i guess that does happen”), and by 2025 @AndrewCurran_ jokes the AI-era version is simply refusing to deviate from your opinions.

Why care: it’s basically a social-security model for belief—who gets to run code in your head, under what permissions, and how you avoid getting voluntold into endless debates where the goal isn’t truth, it’s control.
